Photograph: Henry Nicholls/Reuters View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham in Mykhailivska Square, Kyiv, on 24 August 2026. Photograph: Henry Nicholls/Reuters Opinion Ukraine The Guardian view on Britain helping Ukraine: build the weapons independence Kyiv needs Editorial Moscow hopes western politics will weaken support for Kyiv. The UK and Europe’s answer should be to make Ukraine increasingly capable of defending itself alone Mon 24 Aug 2026 13.53 EDT Last modified on Mon 24 Aug 2026 13.58 EDT Share T he events of the past few days on Europe’s borders may mark a turning point in Russia’s war on Ukraine. While the political skies in Kyiv have darkened for Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the military picture looks brighter. Ukraine can already send swarms of drones against Russian oil facilities, e-commerce warehouses and airfields. Andy Burnham’s arrival in Kyiv marks a step forward. Britain is releasing classified information on its components of Scalp , the French version of the Anglo-French Storm Shadow cruise missile, enabling its assembly in Ukraine. This is more than another weapon for Kyiv. Britain is helping Ukraine become less dependent on the western armoury. Moscow sabre-rattles , but Britain should hold its nerve. Kyiv has been at the mercy of its allies, waiting to replenish weapons stockpiles and release sophisticated arms. Producing its own hi-tech armoury gives Ukraine greater freedom of action because western governments have let go. Two years ago it was different. Joe Biden waited until November 2024 before letting Ukraine strike deep into Russia with US weapons. Yet thresholds once deemed dangerously escalatory have since been crossed without provoking a Russia-Nato war. Kyiv is now being trusted with something more consequential: a measure of weapons independence. View image in fullscreen Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Photograph: Maxym Marusenko/EPA It needs this. Ukraine cannot overcome its manpower disadvantage by fighting Russia soldier for soldier for every kilometre of its vital eastern fortress belt, where Kyiv is losing ground . If Moscow can freely push ammunition, drones and equipment towards Donetsk, eventually something will give. Cruise missiles offer another strategy, making it harder and costlier for Russian forces to reach the front. Europe is thinking defensively too. Ukraine relies heavily on the US-made Patriots to down ballistic missiles, but global shortages of interceptors, a situation made worse by the US war with Iran, have left it exposed. With European help, Ukraine’s defence industry is developing an anti-ballistic system intended to reduce that dependence. Kyiv is ramping up its own ballistic missiles. If both are successful, Ukraine would be better able both to strike and defend itself without first appealing to Washington. War is a terrible thing, but what is the alternative? Moscow offers little evidence that territorial success would satisfy it. Despite enormous casualties and painfully slow advances, Vladimir Putin rejects proposals that fail to meet Russia’s broader conditions while expanding military power rather than preparing his people for compromise. Then there is the rise of the far right in Europe, large parts of which are pro-Russia . If Mr Putin thinks that the outlook for Russia’s position will improve politically over the next two or three years, he will bargain harder. Why accept merely the Donbas today if the coalition supporting Ukraine might be weaker tomorrow? That option disappears if either Russia’s war burden becomes intolerable or the west convincingly insulates its material help from political change. History offers lessons. In Vladislav M Zubok’s Collapse: The Fall of the Soviet Union, Boris Yeltsin is startled to hear that Ukrainians, including millions of Russian speakers, want independence in 1991. Once convinced this is their democratic will, however, he accepts it. Russia, he says, will “recognise this new political reality”. Mr Putin starts from the same sense of historical intimacy and reaches the opposite conclusion: that Ukraine’s democratic choices cannot override Russia’s claim to a privileged role in its future. That is a revanchist error he ought to regret. The Eastern Flank Working in Romania New Names on the Cover The Cooking Show Expat in Romania RRI Special The Sounds of Romania Voices from the Archives Our Shows Listeners’ Corner Romanian without Tears Sunday Show In the Spotlight Through the Looking Glass Change Makers Happening in Romania Music Time Artscape Weekend Edition On demand LISTEN HERE Useful information Things to know How to listen Forum QSL QSL-cards Homepage » News and Current Affairs » Newsflash » AUGUST 15, 2026 AUGUST 15, 2026 A roundup of local and world news Newsflash Newsroom , 15.08.2026, 13:59 HOLIDAY Christians are today celebrating the Assumption of Mary or St. Mary, considered the patron saint of sailors, a holiday, which reminds us how the Virgin Mary left this world. The Assumption of the Virgin Mary is the patron saint of most monasteries in Romania and because of that the aforementioned holiday is reason for the biggest pilgrimages in this country. Structures with the Romanian Interior Ministry have deployed additional personnel to contribute to public safety in the Romanian Black Sea resorts presently in full holiday season. Their mission is to ensure the public order at the events occasioned by the Navy Day but also to ease road traffic and for rapid intervention in emergency situations. Policemen are present around the worship places as well. MESSAGES ‘In the past years, the Black Sea has become a crucial area for Europe’s security’ Romanian President, Nicusor Dan, says in his Navy Day address. “The Black Sea is an area where Romania is affirming its strategic interests and projecting its future”, the Head of the Romanian state went on to say. “The Black Sea means trade, energy and connectivity.” “The war in Ukraine proved that Romania is not at the edge of the European Union, Romania is the Union’s first defence line; we are in the Eastern Flank, at the EU’s most important border, the border between a free Europe and a country where citizens are defending their freedom with the price of their lives, and that obliges us,” Romania’s acting Defence Minister says during the ceremonies in Constanta. “It obliges us, Radu Miruta says, because peace is not kept by hoping that others do not attack us, peace is kept by equipping ourselves and making others realize that if they attack us, there will be a heavy price to pay.” “I am here to thank all those who are vigilant on the sea so that we can sleep safe and sound on the ground, to thank all those who support these people, their families, ship builders, port workers, all our partners with whom we cooperate for the security of our eastern border and in the Black Sea”, the acting Prime Minister, Ilie Bolojan says. AMENDMENTS This weekend, the Labour Ministry submitted to the Presidential Administration a series of fresh amendments to the Public Sector Wage Law. President Nicusor Dan has asked for these amendments ahead of a new meeting with the political leaders with a view to reaching an agreement on endorsing and promulgating the law by August 31, the deadline assumed through the PNRR. According to the acting Labour Minister, Dragos Pislaru, the present version has been significantly improved in two areas, healthcare and education. The Minister also says the amendments are targeting the salary scale for high-ranking officials. He says he has received the salary scale by e-mail from the Chamber of Deputies, and that it was agreed upon by the leaders of the political Parliamentary groups. According to him, the interim government cannot amend this proposal. 770 million Euros worth of European funds are hinging on the endorsement of the aforementioned law. DAY Romania’s Naval Forces are celebrating Navy Day today—an event marked in six cities: Constanţa, Mangalia, Brăila, Tulcea, Galaţi, and Bucharest. As in previous years, the Black Sea port city of Constanţa is the central point of the celebration; over 3,500 Romanian and foreign military personnel are participating in the military ceremony and the joint naval exercise led by the Romanian Naval Forces, attended by acting Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan and acting Minister of Defence Radu Miruţă. The ceremony began with the hoisting of the ensign, the jack, and the full dress ship flags aboard the military vessels, while maritime activities kicked off with the traditional arrival of the god Neptune, accompanied by nautical games taking place along the waterfront. The newest vessel to enter service with the Romanian Navy, the corvette ‘Contra-admiral August Roman’, fired the opening salute for the joint naval exercise, which includes sequences involving mine countermeasures, repelling enemy air attacks, searching for and attacking enemy submarines, repelling an amphibious landing, combating illegal migration, and maritime search and rescue operations. A total of over 50 ships and boats, military and civil aircraft, amphibious armored personnel carriers, and artillery pieces are participating, involving the Naval Forces, the Coast Guard, the Romanian Agency for Saving Human Lives at Sea, the General Inspectorate for Emergency Situations, and the Romanian Air Club. Ships from Turkey and Bulgaria are present, along with two Spanish F-18 aircraft conducting NATO enhanced air policing missions and a French Navy Atlantique 2 maritime patrol aircraft. The evening will conclude with a military concert, a torchlight procession by the sailors, as well as a laser and light show. PNRR Romania has officially submitted payment request No. 5 under the NRRP, totaling 2.84 billion Euros, the interim Minister of Investments and European Projects, Dragoş Pîslaru has announced. This request covers 75 targets and milestones (21 reforms and 54 investments), comprising a net value of 1.65 billion euros in non-repayable European funds (grants) and 433 million euros in loans. This is the penultimate payment request under the NRRP. With this submission, Romania reaches a 78% absorption rate for the grant component. Romania’s Recovery and Resilience Plan is funded with 21.41 billion euros, consisting of 13.57 billion euros in grants and 7.84 billion in loans. https://www.politico.eu/article/russias-.text: Moscow is moving to expand its capacity to make tens of thousands of the killer drones it deploys in attacks on Ukrainian cities, according to plans from a Russian state company obtained by POLITICO. The expansion of state firm Rosatom’s Alabuga-Volokno factory in Russia’s Tatarstan region would allow Moscow to make an additional 500 tons of military-grade aerospace carbon fiber each year by 2029. The strong lightweight material is key to building the drone’s airframe. The production increase would translate to an additional 28,000 weaponized drones every year, according to one expert estimate — a 78% increase in production of weapons like the one that struck a passenger train on the Polish border this month and others that have left scores of Ukrainian civilians dead. Ukraine estimates Russia can currently produce more than 36,000 kamikaze drones , known as “Gerans,” annually. Advertisement Advertisement The plans underscore Russia's commitment to weaponized drone technology to power its war machine, which it is increasingly turning against the rest of Europe . The Alabuga-Volokno factory and its parent company, Rosatom’s advanced materials division UMATEX, are sanctioned by the U.K., U.S. and multiple other Western governments. The factory is a key node in Moscow’s military-industrial supply chain and is the same one that received a disguised shipment of 46 tons of carbon-fiber chemicals from a Chinese-state corporation earlier this year, according to internal Rosatom shipping and customs documents reported earlier this month by POLITICO. Rosatom previously said the firm and its subsidiaries “operate in full compliance” with applicable laws and regulations. Police experts examine fragments of a drone which targeted a commuter train, killing one and wounding eight people, in the Kharkiv region on September 18, 2026 amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. | Sergey Bobok/ AFP via Getty Images The Chinese embassy in Washington said in a statement that it was unaware of the Russian drone production expansion plans and “strictly controls exports of dual use items in accordance with law.” Business, design and structural plans gathered from Russian sources by the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Centre — a Kyiv-based think tank close to the Ukrainian government — detail the factory’s expansion and schematics for its equipment and construction. Rosatom declined to comment on the documents. Advertisement Advertisement The U.S. House Select Committee on China has reviewed the documents and determined they are authentic, according to a U.S. government official familiar with their contents. The Ukrainian government has also reviewed the documents and confirmed their authenticity, a Ukrainian official said. Both officials were granted anonymity as they were not authorized to speak on the record. Russia's drone war expands In May, the Russian government approved Rosatom’s plans to build the new line at its Alabuga-Volokno factory “for the production of chemical fibers and threads” to produce up to 500 tons of carbon fiber per year, according to official approval for the construction project. Satellite images between May and July show land earmarked for the expansion project adjacent to Alabuga-Volokno’s current carbon fiber factory in Tatarstan being cleared for construction, said the Ukrainian official. The images provided by the USCC show “proof that it is already growing,” this official said. The foundation of the new factory “is being prepared,” said weapons expert David Albright, founder and president of the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security think tank, who independently obtained satellite images of the site from August. The timeline for the factory’s completion in 2027, he said, “requires rapid construction.” Drones allow Moscow to “launch these massive volleys and put pressure on deep targets within Ukraine at many different locations, and ensure that they can saturate the defenses,” said Stacie Pettyjohn, a former adviser in the Office of the Secretary of Defense who researches drone warfare at the Center for a New American Security in Washington. “It's been a very good coercive tool and critical to Russia's deep strike campaign.” Rosatom’s plans to grow its capacity to feed Russia’s demands to increase weaponized drone production isn’t just a concern for Ukraine as Moscow’s fifth year of all-out war drags into another winter. Advertisement Advertisement “The expansion of Alabuga and its affiliated enterprises should be viewed not merely as a problem for the Ukrainian front, but as a long-term challenge to the security of the whole of Europe,” said Serhii Kuzan, head of the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Centre. In-housing production Moscow is working to increase its domestic carbon fiber production to reduce its reliance on imports from China as it aims to manufacture around 130,000 drones for its national “Unmanned Aerial Systems” project by 2030, according to an analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington-based think tank, this year . Russia plans to increase this to 350,000 by 2035. Rosatom’s Alabuga-Volokno will aid this national effort. The three key reasons for expanding the factory include “import substitution of dual-use products” and “meeting the demand of Russian strategic sectors (aviation, defense industry) for carbon fiber,” according to the Rosatom documents. The factory’s total capacity “could make 28,000 Shahed 136 drone airframes,” calculates weapons expert Albright, whose Institute for Science and International Security has conducted years of in-depth research on Russia’s drone production. Russia’s Geran-2 attack drones are based on the design of Iran’s Shahed. “Without the carbon fiber, they can't make the drone,” Albright said. Russia “can't substitute for the carbon fiber in the drone and keep its weight down,” he explained, noting the material is used to strengthen the wing and internal structures, such as those for the fuel tank and engine. Moscow is not getting enough polyacrylonitrile tow — a so-called PAN-precursor — used to make high-spec carbon fiber “for all their defense needs,” Albright said. Through the factory, Moscow is attempting to reduce its reliance on imports of the fibrous chemical essential to reinforcing its drones’ airframe. Advertisement Advertisement The internal Rosatom plans show the firm intends to build a new “a modern PAN plant” in Tatarstan’s Alabuga Special Economic Zone factory complex. “The project's primary product will be UMT42S-3K grade carbon fiber,” the documents detail, to be “used in the aerospace industry.” Metadata scraped from the document shows it was created by an employee of Russian state corporation Rosatom’s advanced materials division UMATEX at the end of last year. Drones produced in the Alabuga SEZ complex have become a key part of Moscow’s strategy of targeting both the Ukrainian military and civilians. “Monitoring, restricting the supply of critical components, sanctions enforcement, disrupting logistics chains and reducing the production resilience of this complex must be among the priorities of the joint policy of Ukraine and its European partners,” said USCC’s Kuzan. “At this stage, the Kremlin’s hybrid aggression is increasingly shifting towards direct escalation, particularly through the conduct of so-called sub-threshold actions, aimed at gauging the reaction of European countries,” he said, pointing to documented violations by Russian drones of Polish and Romanian airspace. Moscow has now also added jet engines to Russia’s design of its Geran drones — allowing it to strike further and faster. Drones manufactured in the Russian Alabuga Special Economic Zone, Kuzan warned, “are likely to become the main instrument of the Russian Federation’s future campaigns in Europe.” Advertisement Advertisement The Russian embassy in Washington didn’t respond to a request for comment. Europe at risk With no end in sight for the Ukraine war and as Russia increases its attacks at NATO's eastern fringe, world leaders gather this week in New York City for the annual United Nations General Assembly. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said last week that Moscow is ready to restart negotiations to end its war, according to state-owned media outlet TASS . In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov attends the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 12, 2026. | Alexander Kazavok/ AFP via Getty Images Early this month, Russia’s permanent representative to the U.N., Vasily Nebenzya, reportedly led an unsuccessful effort to remove an item titled the “Situation in the Temporarily Occupied Territories of Ukraine” from the upcoming UNGA agenda. Revelations of the carbon fiber factory’s planned expansion mean Lavrov’s overtures should be approached with skepticism, said Nicholas Fenton, associate director for the Europe, Russia and Eurasia Program at CSIS. The September drone attack on the passenger train close to the Polish border and a series of examples of hybrid warfare in Europe — like sabotage and other tactics that fall below the threshold of open warfare — show Moscow has “significant appetite” to escalate the conflict both in Ukraine and Europe, Fenton said. Advertisement “No matter the political outcome over some sort of diplomatic solution to Ukraine, we don't see Russia de-escalating when it comes to its military posture vis-à-vis NATO or vis-à-vis Europe,” Fenton said. “We believe that the current leadership of the regime in Russia is committed to confrontation with the West,” he said — even if a peace deal is struck. At the start of September, President Donald Trump dispatched U.S. special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff to Moscow and Kyiv to jumpstart a peace process. These visits reaped “substantive progress including movement on scheduling additional trilateral talks,” Witkoff wrote online afterward. Yet Russia killed five people in missile and drone attacks on Kyiv just a day after Trump's envoys left. Moscow has continued drone attacks on civilian infrastructure across Ukraine since. “The Russians are gaining momentum in the air war, continuing to iterate these systems, continuing to expand production,” Fenton said. “There's significant concern over what might be coming.” Graham Lanktree reported from London. Phelim Kine reported from Washington.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6n8.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, File photo from 2021 of a beach in northern France used by migrants to attempt the Channel crossing to England By Hugh Schofield in Paris Published 4 hours ago Six people traffickers have been found guilty in France of causing the deaths of 31 migrants in the worst ever small-boat accident in the Channel. At the end of a four-week trial in Paris, the six were convicted of "involuntary homicide" and given prison terms of between six and 10 years. Seven others were given lesser sentences of up to four years, and one person was found not guilty. The boat went down early in the morning on 24 November 2021 after sending distress calls to French and British coastguards. The dead, including a child of seven, were mainly Iraqi Kurds but also included Afghans, Egyptians and Iranian Kurds. Only two men survived. The charge sheet said the migrants had been put to sea from the French coast in a boat "that was of poor quality, uncertified, unsuitable for navigation at sea, overloaded, and without correct life jackets". The trial established that the guilty men were members of two separate networks â one of which was Iraqi Kurd, the other Afghan â that co-operated to organise the cross-channel journey and bring migrants to the meeting point. Unusually the court was attended at the start by several family members, who came to France from Iraqi Kurdistan and gave moving testimony about how the victims came to be on board the boat. Image caption, Some of the victims (from left): Mohammed Hussein Mohammedie, Mhabad Ahmad Ali, Bilind Shakir Baker, Shakar Ali Pirot, Bryar Hamad Abdulrahman, and Hasti Rizghar Hussein Speaking after the verdict, their lawyer Matthieu Chirez said the decision "comes as a relief for all the civil plaintiffs because it confirms the penal responsibility of the traffickers". He said the trial had "humanised the families of victims". One family member, Zana Marmand Muhammed, told the court how his younger brother Twana had "wanted to go to England to find a job and because the geopolitical situation with us is dangerous. No-one in the family wanted him to leave, but we could not dissuade him." Nabi Mustafa Mina, the father of Zanyar who was 19 when he died, told of how he tried to dissuade his son from leaving. "I said I would help him to get married, I would give him my house, I would divide my salary in two. But no, he said he wanted a better life, that he would get by somehow. I ran out of arguments," he said. The family-members explained how they had paid a deposit at a bank in Iraqi Kurdistan and then followed their loved ones' progress through Turkey, Italy and then France. In one of the last messages from Twana, he posted a picture of himself at the Eiffel Tower. The court also heard a statement from one of the two survivors, Issa Omar, read out by his lawyer. Omar said that he "would have liked to appear before the judge but I do not have the strength. Since the wreck I have the impression that part of me disappeared beneath the waves." His lawyer Matthieu Chirez said that Omar had "clung to floating bodies, to a life-jacket. He survived by keeping his eyes open so as not to go to sleep, and swimming to keep his heart beating". Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Lawyer Matthieu Chirez (C) said the verdict had come as a relief to victims' families Police investigating the disaster used phone tracking to identify members of the two networks. The lesser figures were accused of sheltering migrants, transporting them across France to the so-called "jungle" camp outside Calais, and helping on the night of the departure. The alleged leader of the Iraqi Kurd network â named as Bashdar â was not a defendant in the trial. He is in custody in Iraq. His close aide â Harem Ahmed Abawaker â was given eight years in prison. The biggest sentence, of 10 years, went to Obaidullah Maroofkhel, who ran the Afghan network. He was tried in his absence along with one other defendant. Most of the 14 were Afghans or Iraqi Kurds. All but one of the defendants appeared in the trial as free men, so following the verdict the court issued six arrest warrants. A separate police investigation is under way into seven members of the French armed forces for allegedly failing to come to the help of the migrants on the night of the disaster. The seven were at the regional sea rescue centre or on board a navy ship, and are alleged to have ignored distress calls from the boat. A decision on whether to recommend them for trial will be taken in the coming months. The trial ended as France and the UK announced it was ending the so-called one-in one-out scheme under which the British government sent back irregular cross-Channel migrants to France, and in return accepted individuals with a likely prospect of being granted asylum. France had already signalled that the year-long programme, which has seen a little more than 1,000 migrants switch country, was not producing expected results in breaking the traffickers' business model. https://cyprus-mail.com/2026/10/13/chris.text: President Nikos Christodoulides on Tuesday stressed that he will attend the Cop31 climate summit, which will take place in the Turkish Mediterranean coastal city of Antalya next month, despite Turkey not recognising him as a head of state. “Of course I will attend. The Republic of Cyprus always attends these summits. I am pleased that, thanks to the decisive contribution of our partners, and following our diplomatic and political efforts conducted away from the public eye, we have achieved a result,” he said. He then stressed that “we have done so without fanfare or publicity”, and that his invite “is a development which also sends messages regarding the Cyprus problem”. Asked whether he may also be expecting “unpleasant surprises” during the summit, he said that “we are preparing for any eventuality, and I must tell you that we do not rule one out”. “At the same time, there will also be reactions from the Republic of Cyprus’ side, a member state of the European Union, of the EU which has 27 member states,” he said. Turkey has been designated as a co-host for the summit, alongside Australia, with Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum designated as the chairman of Cop31 and Australian Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen set to preside over negotiations between political leaders at the Antalya summit. A host country does not have the right to unilaterally exclude any United Nations member state from the negotiations, but it is expected that a series of other events and agreements will be held and reached during the 12-day event in November. Earlier in the year, news website Politico quoted diplomats as having said that Turkey did not invite Cyprus to a Cop31 briefing in New York, and then objected when Cypriots attempted to attend the briefing alongside the EU’s delegation. Sources said ‘Ankara is under no obligation to invite an entity it does not recognise’ At the time, Turkish newspaper Hurriyet had reported that Turkish officials had “rejected the criticism, asserting that Ankara is under no obligation to invite an entity it does not recognise diplomatically”. The newspaper added that Turkey “reiterated its longstanding position on the Cyprus issue, emphasising that Greek Cyprus does not represent the entirety of the island”. Meanwhile, Reuters quoted Turkish diplomatic sources as having said that Cypriot delegations had been invited to “all Cop31-related events under the coordination of the UN”. Those sources, it reported, had said that the New York briefing had been organised by the Turkish government independently of the Cop structure. “The various contacts and meetings conducted by our country in the lead-up to Cop31 are events organised at the national level for purposes of preparation, consultation, and promotion,” the sources are quoted as having said. Nonetheless, European Climate Commissioner Wokpe Hoekstra was keen to set his stall out as early as June, warning at the time that “we are not going to accept” the prospect of Cyprus not being invited to the summit. “The full solidarity of the other 26 will apply,” he said, in reference to the EU’s 26 other member states, adding that “there are 27 member states that need to be treated in the same way”, and that “this is a union of 27, full stop”. Likewise, Poland’s secretary of state for climate affairs Krysztof Bolesta said that “if Cyprus is unfairly treated, we should not be going to Turkey”, while Irish Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien told Reuters that his country stands in “full solidarity with Cyprus”, and that “this situation doesn’t need to escalate”.
